annotations.title: Check whether a web page really contains a quote

description: Use when a quote, a statistic or a claim is attributed to a web page and the user asks whether the source says it, or before a citation goes into an answer, report, article or essay (signals: "does this article actually say", "verify this quote", "is this citation real", "check the source", "did they really write that", "fact-check this quote against the link"). Fetches the page once, extracts its visible text and returns per quote a verdict: exact (word for word), normalized (same words in order; only punctuation, capitals, spacing or curly quotes differ), close (similarity 0.85 or more, wording differs), partial (0.5 to 0.85) or not_found, with the matching passage, surrounding context, the words that differ and numbers_differ when a number changed (for example 1914 in the quote, 1912 on the page). Quotes with "..." are checked part by part. Example: {"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing","quotes":["widely regarded as the father of theoretical computer science"]}. Limits: a match shows the words are on the page, not that the claim is true; pages built by JavaScript may have little text in their HTML; PDFs and paywalled or bot-blocked pages cannot be read; up to 10 quotes of 1000 characters, at least 3 words each.

quotes.description: 1 to 10 quotes or claims to look for, as written in the draft (at least 3 words each).

url.description: The http or https address of the source page (an article, doc, blog post, Wikipedia page or plain-text file).

name: vouch_check_quote
